name: District of Columbia

notes: Food that SNAP can buy, and food for animals, is exempt whether or not bought with SNAP, candy included (the snack-food tax was repealed); soft drinks pay 8%, food from vending machines 6% and prepared food 10%, which isn't counted here.
Alcohol sold to take away pays 10.25%; per-gallon excise taxes paid by wholesalers (beer $2.79 a barrel, wine 30 to 45 cents a gallon, spirits $1.50 a gallon) are left out.

Cigarettes and other tobacco pay no sales tax: wholesalers pay a surtax "in lieu of sales tax" (58 cents a pack from October 1, 2026, on top of the $4.50 excise) and 58% of the wholesale price on other tobacco and vapor products (tax year 2027), taxes by the unit or on the wholesale price, left out here.
Household supplies: diapers, adult incontinence products included, are exempt, which is not taken out here.
Pets and toys: pet food is exempt, which is not taken out here: the Economic Census reports pet food with pet supplies, so no share is published.
Personal care products: menstrual products are exempt, which is not taken out here; medicines are exempt with or without a prescription (outside this category); toothpaste and mouthwash are taxed.
Barber and beauty services: haircuts and other barber and beauty services aren't taxed; tanning is (6%), which is not counted here.
Clothing is taxed in full; DC has no sales tax holiday.
Laundry and dry cleaning: laundering, dry cleaning and pressing are taxed, except at self-service coin-operated laundries, which is not taken out here.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and pays a per-gallon tax instead (35.7 cents for tax year 2026), left out here.
Auto repair labor: repairs, the labor of installing parts included, are taxed.

DC has no separate local sales taxes; all rates are District rates. The general rate is 6% through September 30, 2027: the rise to 7% was postponed a year, to October 1, 2027 (Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Act, as the Office of Tax and Revenue and the fiscal impact statement give it; the codified D.C. Code 47-2002 still read 7% from October 1, 2026 when read on October 31, 2026).
Hotel stays pay 15.95%, parking 18% and car rentals 12% from October 1, 2026; soft drinks bought in stores pay 8%. None is counted here.
gaps: The District of Columbia has no local sales taxes; one set of rates applies everywhere. The general rate is 6% through September 30, 2027: the rise to 7% was postponed a year, to October 1, 2027 (Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Act; Office of Tax and Revenue). Restaurant meals and drinks served pay 10% (9% sales tax and 1% for the Washington Convention Center Authority) and alcohol bought in stores pays 10.25%, both counted here. Soft drinks bought in stores pay 8%, not counted. Cigarettes and other tobacco pay no sales tax at the register (a 58-cent-a-pack surtax in lieu of sales tax plus the $4.50 excise, and 58% of the wholesale price on other tobacco and vapor products, all paid by wholesalers); none is counted. Hotel stays pay 15.95%, parking 18% and car rentals 12% from October 1, 2026; not counted.

programs: DC Main Streets' 29 corridors (Department of Small and Local Business Development) and its business improvement districts are mapped from DC GIS. Tax increment financing areas are mapped from DC GIS too, The Wharf's (tax increment and payment in lieu of taxes financing, to 2040) included; Gallery Place isn't shown, since the layer gives its financing as matured in 2017 while the Office of Revenue Analysis' 2025 Dedicated Taxes Report lists it among the areas repaying bonds in fiscal 2024. Three new tax increment areas in the Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Support Act, as its fiscal impact statement describes them (July 2026), have no maps yet: Northeast Heights (up to $47 million), Bryant Street Phase 2 ($26 million) and the Frank D. Reeves Municipal Center ($32 million); whether the final act kept all three wasn't confirmed.

warn.text: Washington draws many visitors (the National Mall and the federal core, downtown and Georgetown), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy over the city as a whole: its seasonal homes (0.8%) and its 374 lodging places (0.5 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs, though 11 of its 206 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
